title: Char Siu
subtitle: Chinese BBQ pork with a sticky, caramelised glaze
excerpt: Char siu is Cantonese roasted pork glazed repeatedly with hoisin sauce, honey and five spice until the outside is lacquered and deeply caramelised. The cut of choice is pork shoulder or neck, which stays juicy even at high heat. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Char siu has been documented in Cantonese cookery since at least the Qing dynasty, and recipes appear in Yue Sai Kan's mid-twentieth century guides to Chinese cooking published in Hong Kong. The dish is discussed at length in Eileen Yin-Fei Lo's 'The Dim Sum Book' (Crown, 1982), which traces its origins to the roasted-meat stalls of Guangzhou and notes that maltose syrup was the traditional sweetener before honey became widely available.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely, slice or leave whole, and freeze in a sealed bag for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat in a hot oven for 8 minutes, brushing with a little extra honey.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate the pork for up to 24 hours in the fridge. The flavour deepens considerably with a longer soak.
recipe.temperatureNote: Start high to caramelise, then drop to 180°C to finish cooking through.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cantonese for 'fork roasted', referring to the traditional method of hanging strips of seasoned pork over a fire on long forks. Today it is made in a domestic oven but the sticky, lacquered glaze and slightly charred edges remain its defining features.

A Chinese fermented rice wine named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. It has a rich, slightly nutty flavour and is used in marinades and sauces throughout Chinese cooking. Dry sherry makes a reasonable substitute.

A ground spice blend typically containing star anise, cloves, Chinese cinnamon, Sichuan pepper and fennel seeds. It balances sweet, sour, salty, bitter and pungent notes and appears in marinades, braises and spice rubs across Chinese cuisine.

A thick, sweet-savoury sauce made from fermented soybean paste, garlic, vinegar and spices. The name translates loosely as 'seafood sauce', though it contains no seafood. It is used as a glaze, dipping sauce and marinade throughout Cantonese and southern Chinese cooking.

content.text: This recipe makes enough
char siu

to serve 4 people as part of a meal with rice, and takes about 1 hour in the oven after a minimum 4-hour marinade. The glaze goes on in several layers during cooking, which is what creates that deep, almost mahogany colour.

Pork neck or shoulder is the right cut here because the fat running through the meat bastes it from the inside. Pork loin will dry out. If you can find maltose syrup at a Chinese grocer, use it in place of honey for a stickier, less sweet glaze, but honey works very well. A splash of
shaoxing wine
in the marinade gives the pork a deeper, more rounded flavour.
What you need
Method

Mix the hoisin sauce, honey, soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, five-spice powder, and red fermented tofu together in a bowl. Add the pork and turn to coat. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight.
Add the pork strips and turn to coat thoroughly. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight for best results.

Heat the oven to 220°C. Line a roasting tin with foil and set a wire rack over it if you have one. Lift the pork out of the marinade, reserving the marinade, and arrange the strips on the rack or foil.
Roast for 15 minutes at 220°C. The high heat sets the glaze quickly.
Turn the pork, brush generously with the reserved marinade and drop the temperature to 180°C. Roast for a further 15 minutes.
Brush with the extra {{honey}} and return to the oven for 5 to 10 minutes until the glaze is deeply coloured and starting to char at the edges. The internal temperature should reach 72°C.
Rest the pork for 5 minutes before slicing across the grain into pieces about 1cm thick. Serve with steamed rice and a drizzle of any juices from the tin.

items.symptom: The glaze is burning before the pork is cooked through
items.cause: The oven is too hot or the strips are too thick
items.fix: Cover loosely with foil and reduce the temperature to 170°C. Continue cooking until the centre reaches 72°C, then uncover and brush with honey for the last 5 minutes.

items.symptom: The pork is dry and tough
items.cause: Pork loin was used instead of shoulder or neck, or it was overcooked
items.fix: Always use a fatty cut. Check the temperature early, as shoulder can reach 72°C faster than expected in a hot oven.

items.symptom: The glaze is pale and not sticking
items.cause: The pork was not patted dry before roasting, or the marinade was too thin
items.fix: Pat the pork dry before putting it in the oven. If the marinade looks watery, reduce it in a small pan for 2 minutes before using it as a basting liquid.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Char siu is a staple of Cantonese roast-meat shops found across Hong Kong and Guangdong province, where whole strips of glazed pork hang in the window alongside roast duck and soy-poached chicken. At home it appears over rice with a drizzle of sauce, tucked into steamed bao buns, or folded through
hoisin sauce
-dressed noodles. The
chinese five spice
and long marinade are what set it apart from other glazed roast pork recipes.
